How robust a company is, and what it could withstand

Source: R/xbrl_robustness.R
xbrl_robustness.Rd

Takes a panel from xbrl_panel() (or xbrl_ratios()) and says, for each company and year, which of the known signs of financial vulnerability it shows, and how large a fall its figures could absorb.

Usage

xbrl_robustness(p, group = "class")

Arguments

p

A panel from xbrl_panel(), or its xbrl_ratios().

group

Columns that make companies comparable, for weak_return. Default "class"; see xbrl_ratios().

Value

p with the factor columns, n_factors, gross_profit_buffer and cash_months added, and the validation in attr(r, "validation").

The factors

Each is a logical column, NA where the figures to judge it are missing:

  • negative_equity – equity below nought.

  • capital_lost – equity below half the contributed capital: the point at which Danish company law requires the board to act.

  • thin_equity – an equity ratio under 15%.

  • two_losses – a loss this year and the year before.

  • shortterm_heavy – short-term debt over half the assets.

  • weak_interest_cover – operating profit under 1.5 times the finance expenses.

  • weak_return – an operating return 5 percentage points or more under the median of comparable companies the same year (see group).

  • young – founded less than five years before the end of the year.

  • going_concern_factor – the auditor, or the filing itself, reports a material uncertainty about the company continuing. Where an auditor audited or reviewed the accounts and said nothing, it is FALSE. Where no auditor looked, it is NA.

They are the variables of Danmarks Nationalbank's bankruptcy model (Finansiel stabilitet 2005), with capital lost and going concern added because a filing states them. n_factors counts those that are TRUE.

What it could withstand

  • gross_profit_buffer – how far the gross profit could fall, as a share, before the operating profit is gone, if staff costs and depreciation did not move. They usually fall a little with it, so this is the smaller end of the buffer. NA where there is no operating profit to lose.

  • cash_months – how many months of staff costs the cash covers.

Have the factors held?

A company that stops filing while the corpus goes on has most often ceased, so the factors can be held against that. attr(r, "validation") compares, for each factor, the share of companies that filed no further annual report within two years, with the factor and without it, over the years for which two later years are in the data. It is a proxy: a company can also stop filing because it moved its year end, merged, or left the data for a reason of the data's. It says whether a factor points the right way, not how likely a failure is.

Over 4,304 filings for 2020-2024, 4 to 6% of company-years without a given factor were followed by no annual report within two years. With weak interest cover, a weak return or capital lost it was 2.6 to 2.7 times as many; with negative equity, two losses or a going concern uncertainty about twice. Short-term debt (1.8), thin equity (1.5) and youth (1.4) point the same way, more weakly. By the count of factors: 4.8% with none, 13.5% with four or more.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
r <- xbrl_robustness(xbrl_panel(read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")))
r[r$n_factors >= 3, c("cvr", "name", "period_end", "n_factors")]
attr(r, "validation")
} # }
